title: Serious things breed sects
source_text: Εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ ὡς κατηγορῶν τοῦ λόγου τὰ περὶ τῶν ἐν χριστιανισμῷ αἱρέσεων ὀνειδίζει ἡμῖν λέγων· εἰς πλῆθος δὲ σπαρέντες αὖθις αὖ σχίζονται καὶ τέμνονται καὶ στάσεις ἰδίας ἔχειν ἕκαστοι θέλουσι· φησὶ δ᾿ ὅτι καὶ ὑπὸ πλήθους πάλιν διϊστάμενοι σφᾶς αὐτοὺς ἐλέγχουσιν· ἑνὸς ὡς εἰπεῖν ἔτι κοινωνοῦντες, εἴ γε κοινωνοῦσι, τοῦ ὀνόματος, καὶ τοῦτο μόνον ἐγκαταλιπεῖν ὅμως αἰσχύνονται· τὰ λοιπὰ δ᾿ ἄλλοι ἀλλαχῇ τετάχαται· καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο φήσομεν ὅτι οὐδενὸς πράγματος, οὗ μὴ σπουδαία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀρχὴ καὶ τῷ βίῳ χρήσιμος, γεγόνασιν αἱρέσεις διάφοροι, ἐπεὶ γὰρ ἰατρικὴ χρήσιμος καὶ ἀναγκαία τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων, πολλά τε τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ζητούμενα περὶ τοῦ τρόπου τῆς τῶν σωμάτων θεραπείας, διὰ τοῦτο αἱρέσεις ἐν ἰατρικῇ παρὰ μὲν Ἕλλησιν εὑρίσκονται ὁμολογουμένως πλείονες, ἐγὼ δ᾿ οἶμαι ὅτι καὶ παρὰ βαρβάροις, ὅσοι (γε) ἐπαγγέλλονται χρῆσθαι ἰατρικῇ, πάλιν τε αὖ ἐπεὶ φιλοσοφία ἀλήθειαν ἐπαγγελλομένη καὶ γνῶσιν τῶν ὄντων πῶς δεῖ βιοῦν ὑποτίθεται καὶ πειρᾶται διδάσκειν τὰ ὠφέλιμα ἡμῶν τῷ γένει, πολλὴν δ᾿ ἔχει τὰ ζητούμενα πράγματα διολκὴν, διὰ τοῦτο αἱρέσεις ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ συνέστησαν πλεῖσται ὅσαι, ὧν αἱ μέν εἰσι διασημότεραι αἱ δὲ οὐ τοιαῦται, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἰουδαϊσμὸς πρόφασιν ἔσχε γενέσεως αἱρέσεων τὴν διάφορον ἐκδοχὴν τῶν Μω(??)σέως γραμμάτων καὶ τῶν προφητικῶν λόγων. οὕτω τοίνυν, ἐπεὶ σεμνόν τι ἐφάνη τοῖς ἀνθρώποις χριστιανισμὸς, οὐ μόνοις, ὡς ὁ Κέλσος οἴεται, τοῖς ἀνδραποδωδεστέροις ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλοῖς τῶν παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι φιλολόγων, ἀναγκαίως ὑπέστησαν οὐ πάντως διὰ (τὰς) στάσεις καὶ τὸ φιλόνεικον αἱρέσεις ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ σπουδάζειν συνιέναι τὰ χριστιανισμοῦ καὶ τῶν φιλολόγων πλείονας, τούτῳ δ᾿ ἠκολούθησε, διαφόρως ἐκδεξαμένων τοὺς ἅμα πᾶσι πιστευθέντας εἶναι θείους λόγους, τὸ γενέσθαι αἱρέσεις ἐπωνύμους τῶν θαυμασάντων μὲν τὴν τοῦ λόγου ἀρχὴν κινηθέντων δ᾿ ὅπως ποτ᾿ οὖν ὑπό τινων πιθανοτήτων πρὸς τὰς εἰς ἀλλήλους διαφωνίας. ἀλλ᾿ οὔτ᾿ ἰατρικὴν εὐλόγως ἄν τις φεύγοι διὰ τὰς ἐν αὐτῇ αἱρέσεις, οὔτε φιλοσοφίαν τοῦ πρέποντος στοχαζόμενός τις ἂν μισοῖ, πρόφασιν τοῦ μισεῖν αὐτὴν ποριζόμενος τὰς πολλὰς αἱρέσεις. οὕτως οὐδὲ διὰ τὰς ἐν Ἰουδαίοις αἱρέσεις καταγνωστέον τῶν Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἱερῶν βιβλίων.
pass_a_gloss: Then since, as accusing (κατηγορῶν) the word, he reproaches (ὀνειδίζει) us with the sects (αἱρέσεις) in Christianity (χριστιανισμός), saying: 'sown into a multitude they again are split (σχίζονται) and cut (τέμνονται) and each wish to have their own factions (στάσεις)'; and he says that 'by the multitude again standing apart (διϊστάμενοι) they refute (ἐλέγχουσιν) themselves, still sharing (κοινωνοῦντες), so to speak, one thing, if indeed they share, the name (ὄνομα), and this alone they are nevertheless ashamed (αἰσχύνονται) to abandon (ἐγκαταλιπεῖν); the rest some are ranged (τετάχαται) one place, others another'; to this we shall say that of no matter (πρᾶγμα) whose principle (ἀρχή) is not serious (σπουδαία) and useful (χρήσιμος) to life have different sects arisen; for since medicine (ἰατρική) is useful and necessary to the human race, and many things are inquired (ζητούμενα) in it about the manner of treatment (θεραπεία) of bodies, therefore sects in medicine are found among Greeks admittedly (ὁμολογουμένως) many, and I think also among barbarians, as many as profess (ἐπαγγέλλονται) to use medicine; and again since philosophy professing truth (ἀλήθεια) and knowledge of beings (γνῶσις τῶν ὄντων) proposes (ὑποτίθεται) how one must live and tries to teach what is beneficial (ὠφέλιμα) to our race, and the questions have much divergence (διολκή), therefore very many sects arose in philosophy, some more distinguished (διασημότεραι), others not; but Judaism too had as pretext (πρόφασις) of the genesis of sects the different interpretation (ἐκδοχή) of the writings of Moses and the prophetic words. So then since Christianity appeared something venerable (σεμνόν) to men, not only, as Celsus thinks, to the more slavish (ἀνδραποδωδέστεροι) but to many of the learned (φιλόλογοι) among Greeks, necessarily (ἀναγκαίως) sects arose, not altogether/by no means (οὐ πάντως) through factions and love of strife (φιλόνεικον), but through more of the learned also being eager (σπουδάζειν) to understand (συνιέναι) the things of Christianity; and on this followed, as they interpreted differently the words believed by all together to be divine, the arising of sects named after (ἐπωνύμους) those who admired the principle of the word but were moved somehow (ὅπως ποτ' οὖν) by certain plausibilities (πιθανότητες) to mutual disagreements (διαφωνίαι). But neither would one reasonably flee medicine for its sects, nor would one aiming at the fitting (τοῦ πρέποντος στοχαζόμενος) hate philosophy, providing the many sects as pretext; so neither must the sacred books (ἱερὰ βιβλία) of Moses and the prophets be condemned (καταγνωστέον) because of the sects among Jews.
pass_b_english: Then, as if bringing a charge against the word, he reproaches us with the sects within Christianity, saying: “But once they had spread into a multitude, they split and are cut apart again, and each group wants factions of its own.” And he says that “being divided again because of their numbers, they refute one another; they still have, so to speak, one thing in common, if indeed they have even that: the name; and this alone they are nevertheless ashamed to abandon; in everything else they are ranged one here, another there.”

To this too we shall say that differing sects have never arisen in any matter unless its first principle is serious and useful to life. Since medicine is useful and necessary to the human race, and many questions are raised in it about how bodies should be treated, for this reason there are admittedly many sects in medicine among the Greeks, and I think also among the barbarians, at least among all who profess to practise medicine. Again, since philosophy professes truth and the knowledge of things that are, lays down how one ought to live, and tries to teach what benefits our race, while the matters it inquires into allow wide differences of view, for this reason a great many sects have arisen in philosophy, some more famous, others less so. And Judaism too found occasion for sects to arise in the differing interpretation of the writings of Moses and the words of the prophets.

So then, since Christianity appeared to people as something worthy of reverence, not only, as Celsus supposes, to the more slavish, but also to many of the learned among the Greeks, sects necessarily arose, not altogether because of factions and love of strife, but because a number of the learned too were eager to understand the teachings of Christianity. From this it followed that, as they interpreted differently the words that all alike believed to be divine, sects arose named after men who admired the first principle of the word, yet were moved somehow by certain plausible arguments to their disagreements with one another.

But no one could reasonably shun medicine because of the sects within it, nor would anyone who aims at what is fitting hate philosophy, using its many sects as a pretext for hating it. So neither should the sacred books of Moses and the prophets be condemned because of the sects among the Jews.

choices.choice: αἱρέσεις is rendered 'sects' throughout (medicine, philosophy, Judaism, Christianity) because Origen's argument depends on the same word for all four; 'medical sects' (Empiricists, Methodists etc.) is the usual English term. The first Celsus quotation repeats 3.10 with the verbs reversed (σχίζονται καὶ τέμνονται), and the order is kept. 'ὑπὸ πλήθους' rendered 'because of their numbers'. 'οὐ πάντως' is ambiguous ('not altogether' or 'by no means'); 'not altogether' keeps the ambiguity. 'τὴν τοῦ λόγου ἀρχήν' rendered 'the first principle of the word' (the Christian message; lowercase). Staging marks editorial supplements (γε) and (τὰς), both accepted; 'Μω(??)σέως' is a staging artefact for Μωϋσέως.
No change: both Celsus quotations (verb order reversed from 3.10, kept), the medicine / philosophy / Judaism parallels, οὐ πάντως, ἐπωνύμους and the closing condemnation clause all match the Greek.
Restructuring of the opening ἐπεί clause into a statement plus 'To this too we shall say' checked: no content lost.
